name: Semantic Router
decomposition_method: None (no decomposition). Semantic Router does not split a compound prompt into sub-tasks. The entire input is embedded as a single vector and matched against route reference utterances. Multi-intent queries are collapsed into one route rather than decomposed, which is the library's primary acknowledged failure mode.
decomposition_granularity: Not applicable. The unit of routing is the whole input utterance mapped to one route; there is no sub-task granularity.
ordering_strategy: Not applicable. A single route is selected per call; there is no ordering of multiple sub-tasks. (A surrounding application could call the router multiple times, but the library provides no ordering logic.)
decomposition_validation: None. With no decomposition step there is no solvability/completeness/non-redundancy check. The closest analog is the per-route score threshold, which validates only whether the single chosen route is confident enough; it cannot detect that a compound prompt contained multiple uncovered intents.
hierarchy_depth: flat. Routes are a flat set of Route objects, each defined by a name plus example utterances. No hierarchical skill tree or nested routing is provided natively.
router_type: single-label classifier via embedding retrieval (kNN). Cosine similarity between the query embedding and route utterance embeddings; top_k nearest utterances are aggregated (max/mean/sum) per route and the highest-scoring route above its threshold wins. routeTopK can return the top-N routes with scores, but the canonical decision returns one route. It is a retrieve-then-aggregate scheme, not a graph planner or multi-label classifier.
routing_model: embedding similarity. Routing is done by an encoder (e.g., OpenAI, Cohere, HuggingFace, FastEmbed, local models) producing embeddings compared by kNN/cosine; no LLM is invoked for the routing decision itself. Dynamic routes optionally add an LLM call after route selection to extract function arguments, but route choice remains embedding-based.
handles_ambiguity: best-effort pick with threshold-gated abstain. The single highest-similarity route above its score_threshold is chosen; if the best score falls below threshold the query is not routed (falls through to a default/None route). By design it cannot represent two simultaneous intents (centroid smearing / multi-intent collapse). No clarification request or POMDP handling.
fallback_behavior: route to default/None (no-match). When no route exceeds its threshold the router returns a null/None route, and the surrounding application decides what to do (commonly fall back to a general LLM). The library itself does not escalate, retry, or re-decompose; a documented production pattern is semantic router as fast path with an LLM as the below-threshold fallback.
skill_pool_scale_and_retrieval: embedding retrieval (top-k) over all routes; scales to many thousands of routes/tools cheaply because matching is vector math, not full-context prompting. Each route is represented by its utterance embeddings; routing latency stays low (~100ms vs seconds for LLM routing). Limitation: each route's representation is essentially a region/centroid of utterance vectors, so a route serving several distinct use-cases in different embedding regions is hard to capture (single-point/centroid limitation). No retrieve-then-rerank LLM stage in the base path.
router_agent_asymmetry: Not applicable in the intended sense. The router matches on route example utterances (developer-authored), not on a skill's full text vs name-only description. There is no router-vs-agent information asymmetry because Semantic Router only selects a route; it does not feed skill descriptions to a downstream executing agent. [uncertain]
execution_pattern: single dispatch (no multi-task execution). The router returns one route name (static) or one route plus LLM-extracted function arguments (dynamic). It does not orchestrate execution of multiple sub-tasks; that is left to the host application.
parallel_vs_concurrent: Not applicable. The router makes one classification per call; any parallelism/concurrency is the host application's responsibility.
dependency_detection: Not applicable. No multi-sub-task model, so no independent-vs-dependent analysis.
result_aggregation: Not applicable to results, but note the kNN score aggregation: per route, the top_k nearest utterance similarities are combined via aggregation method (max default, or mean/sum) to produce the route score. This aggregates similarity scores, not sub-task results.
mid_chain_feedback: none. Routing is a stateless one-shot embedding comparison; there is no plan to re-route based on downstream results within the library.
benchmark_name: No standardized public benchmark bundled. Reported figures are informal: ~90% intent-detection accuracy, comparable to prompt-based intent detection, in third-party/blog evaluations; threshold optimization is evaluated on user-provided utterance/label sets via the fit method. [uncertain]
multi_intent_coverage: Not covered; explicitly a weakness. The router collapses multi-intent queries into a single route by design, so it neither benchmarks nor supports parallel/sequential/mixed multi-intent prompts. This is the stated reason it serves as a baseline rather than a multi-intent solution.
accuracy_metric: exact-match on route name (single-label classification accuracy). Threshold optimization uses route-label match against training utterances X with targets y. Argument-level (AST) or state-based metrics are not part of the core evaluation. [uncertain]
clarification_capability: None. No when-to-ask vs when-to-answer behavior; the only ambiguity signal is the below-threshold no-route outcome, which the application may turn into a clarification, but the library provides no clarification mechanism or metric (no ClarifyBench/InteractComp-style evaluation).
process_vs_outcome_eval: outcome-only (final route correctness); single-step so there are no intermediate process steps to supervise. [uncertain]
eval_stability: Reproducible for the routing step itself because it is deterministic embedding similarity given a fixed encoder; however accuracy drifts when the embedding model is swapped (embedding-space drift) or when reference utterances go stale. No virtual/cached API benchmark concept applies. [uncertain]
integration_pattern: standalone service / in-process library (middleware between user and downstream LLM or agent). Typically deployed as a fast pre-LLM classification layer: embed query, pick route, then dispatch to the corresponding handler, tool, or fallback LLM. Supports many encoders and a vector index; can sit in front of a LangGraph/agent app as a cheap router.
routing_layer: application-layer (Python/Node library). Runs in the application process as a pre-LLM gate; not an inference-engine-layer router itself. (Note: a separate vLLM Semantic Router project pushes similar classification into Envoy/ext_proc, but Aurelio's semantic-router is app-layer.)
latency_overhead: Very low: one embedding call plus vector math, typically ~100ms (vs ~5000ms for LLM-based routing), no LLM round-trip for static routes. Dynamic routes add one LLM call only for argument extraction after the route is chosen. Minimal token cost since routing avoids putting all tools in an LLM context window.
online_adaptation: static at inference; supports offline threshold optimization (fit on labeled utterances) and manual addition of utterances/routes, but no automatic bandit/RL or outcome-feedback learning. It cannot learn that one tool yields better outcomes than another for a query class; reference utterances must be manually refreshed to avoid staleness.
adoption: open-source (with code), production use. aurelio-labs/semantic-router is an actively maintained, widely used MIT-licensed library (Python; community Node port exists), positioned as a fast embedding-based routing layer; commonly used as the cheap fast-path router in production hybrid setups. [uncertain] (license stated as MIT/open-source.)
